You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Stuffing the paper into the cup
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is the source paper visibly stuffed inside the source cup in the edited image?
node.criteria: Pass if the edited image shows the paper from the source image placed inside the cup from the source image, with visible evidence it has been stuffed into it. Fail if the matched paper and cup are assessable and the paper is visibly outside the cup or only resting nearby or on its rim. Unknown if the source objects cannot be reliably matched in the edited image, or their relationship cannot be assessed.
node.binding: Identify the requested paper and cup by their visual and contextual roles in the source image, allowing their appearance to change in the edited image. Judge whether that paper is stuffed inside that cup; do not require exact color or shape matches.

node_traces.evidence: The source paper and cup are visible, but the edited image shows a hand holding a blue printed item near a round object. The source paper and cup cannot be reliably matched to these objects, so whether the paper was stuffed into the cup cannot be established.

fulfillment: The node’s partial result conflicts with the rubric’s reference label, but the trace exposes a more basic issue: the edited image does not reliably show the source white paper or blue cup. It shows a hand holding a blue printed item near a round object, so the claimed match and “partly into the matched cup” progress are unsupported. Tighten the binding to require identity matching against the source objects before crediting completion or progress; when that match is unresolved, preserve unknown rather than inferring progress from proximity. Also inspect the support routing/criteria: the parent is s2 while the decision criteria require both s1 and s2, and the trace treats s2 as sufficient for partial despite s1 being unknown. Ensure the node applies the stated evidence conditions consistently. Do not force “no” from the reference label; it constrains the aggregate but does not establish atomic evidence.
s2: The binding is incomplete and the trace shows why: it credits a blue printed item near a round object as the source paper and cup, despite the source showing a white sheet and a blue cup. Strengthen the node’s source-to-edit identity test: require reliable visual or contextual correspondence for both objects before judging progress, and do not treat color, proximity, or a hand-held item near a round shape as sufficient evidence. If either match or placement is not assessable, return unknown rather than pass or fail. Keep the progress criterion distinct from completion: only count observable movement of the matched paper toward or into the matched cup. Also verify routing and dependency semantics: this support check is parented to s1, yet the trace has no dependencies and appears to determine partial on its own while s1 is unknown. Ensure the node is queried and interpreted consistently with its parent and the aggregate’s evidence requirements. Treat the reference label as an aggregate constraint, not proof that this individual check must be no; separate any execution or routing issue from the visual evidence.
